title: Candidness in Teams Is More Important Topically
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that teams rarely achieve blanket candor, but leaders can still get what they need by asking for full honesty on specific high-stakes topics rather than trying to make every conversation equally frank. It walks through why people self-censor in the first place, from fear of conflict to doubts about their own standing to speak up, and why a positive-team-climate instinct can quietly suppress dissent. The essay's central move is a distinction between broad, low-grade candor and situational, topic-specific candor that a leader can deliberately invoke. It also notes a practical side effect: practicing unfiltered honesty on one issue tends to make people more comfortable being honest elsewhere later. The piece closes with a caution that leaders shouldn't overuse this request, since asking for total candor too often erodes its power.
points: Most people edit themselves out of a desire to be liked, not out of malice or laziness.
It is more valuable for a team to be fully candid on a few critical topics than mildly candid on everything.
Leaders can explicitly ask the team to suspend inhibitions for a single high-stakes discussion.
Practicing candor on one topic builds a habit that carries over to future conversations.
Overusing the request for total candor can wear out its effectiveness.
quotes: It is more important for teams to achieve high levels of candidness topically than it is for them to be somewhat more candid on most issues.
As long as a leader doesn’t go to this well too often, the team will learn to become more candid topically.
Better yet, as they practice this unbridled candor on a given topic, they learn that many of their fears are unfounded and soon become more candid on other matters.
The many reasons people edit themselves and choose not to be candid with others are legion.
Overcoming the obstacles of candor takes time and an unusual trust between team members that can’t be manufactured easily.
